q305.question: How does The Urantia Book interpret the beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount, and how does "brotherly love" differ from "fatherly love"?
q305.answer:
The Urantia Book explains that the words commonly called the "⟦Q 140:4.1⟧Sermon on the Mount⟦/Q⟧" were not the gospel of Jesus as such, but the ordination charge he gave when he set apart the twelve apostles as ambassadors of the kingdom [140:4.1]. It interprets the eight blessings at its opening, the beatitudes, not as a list of laws or duties but as attitudes of living founded on faith and love. In conclusion the narrator says: "⟦Q 140:5.23⟧E assim é revelado que as beatitudes do Sermão da Montanha são baseadas na fé e no amor, e não na lei — na ética ou dever.⟦/Q⟧." [140:5.23]

The key to this interpretation is the distinction between "brotherly love" and "fatherly love." Brotherly love means loving your neighbor as yourself, which fully meets the golden rule, but fatherly love means loving your fellow mortals as Jesus loved us [140:5.1]. Because Jesus lived as a twofold personality, human and divine, he loves mankind as a brother in his capacity as the Son of Man, and as a creator and father in his capacity as the Son of God [140:5.2].

1. The Structure of the Beatitudes: Four Attitudes of Faith

According to The Urantia Book, Jesus first spoke of four faith attitudes as a prelude, and then went on to portray four supreme reactions of fatherly love [140:5.4]. The first four are the poor in spirit, those who hunger for righteousness, the meek, and the pure in heart, and a person who attains these attitudes can arrive at the divine unselfishness needed to practice the Father's affection [140:5.5].

The poor in spirit: Like the publican in the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, these are humble people who do not regard themselves as spiritually rich, who are teachable and seek after God. They find the kingdom of heaven not in some far future but now, within their own hearts [140:5.7].

Those who hunger for righteousness: Only the humble crave spiritual power, and Jesus' righteousness is not the negative "thou shalt not" kind of righteousness but a dynamic love. So it is said: "⟦Q 140:5.9⟧A retidão na experiência é um prazer, não um dever.⟦/Q⟧." [140:5.8-5.9]

The meek: Genuine meekness has nothing to do with fear; it is an attitude of man co-operating with God—"⟦Q 140:5.11⟧Your will be done⟦/Q⟧"—and it springs from an unshakable faith in a lawful and friendly universe [140:5.11].

The pure in heart: Purity is not only a matter of sex attitudes; it is a heart free from suspicion and revenge, an attitude that always looks for the best in people, like the faith of parents in their children. To see God by faith is to gain true spiritual insight, and this strengthens the guidance of the Adjuster and enlarges God-consciousness [140:5.12-5.13].

2. The Four Supreme Reactions of Fatherly Love

The last four show how fatherly love appears in actual living [140:5.15].

Those who mourn: This is not a showy mourning but tenderheartedness. Sympathy is a worthy attribute in men as well, and a sensitive response to human need guards the soul against anger, hate, and suspicion [140:5.16].

The merciful: Mercy here does not mean passive pity; it denotes the height, depth, and breadth of the truest friendship, that is, an active and dynamic fatherliness [140:5.17].

The peacemakers: Jesus' peace is not merely a quiet peace; it is a peace that unifies the individual personality, prevents fear, greed, and anger in society, and prevents suspicion and war between nations [140:5.18].

Those persecuted for righteousness' sake: Fatherly love freely bears sacrifices that brotherly love can hardly endure, and progress has always been the final harvest of persecution [140:5.21].

3. The Call to Perfection

Jesus did not merely tell the apostles to love their neighbors as themselves; he admonished them to love men as he had loved them, saying: "⟦Q 140:5.15⟧“Sede perfeitos, como o vosso Pai nos céus é perfeito”.⟦/Q⟧." [140:5.15] He did not demand of them the impossible manifestation of brotherly love, but he taught that when they strive to be perfect as the Father is, they come to see men as God sees them, and fatherly affection begins [140:5.3]. Since God makes his sun to shine on the evil and the good alike, his children too should be merciful as God is merciful [140:3.16]. Fatherly love delights in returning good for evil [140:5.24].

4. Happiness and Character

The faith and love of these beatitudes strengthen moral character and create happiness, whereas fear and anger weaken character and destroy happiness [140:5.6]. Strong characters are built not by avoiding wrong but by actually doing right, and happy people are motivated not by fear of wrongdoing but by love of right doing [140:4.6]. Fear and shame are unworthy motivations for religious living [140:4.7].

Summary

In The Urantia Book the beatitudes are the heart of the ordination charge given to the apostles, made up of four attitudes of faith (humility, hunger for righteousness, meekness, and purity) and four reactions of fatherly love (tenderheartedness, mercy, peacemaking, and enduring persecution) [140:5.4-5.5, 140:5.15]. If brotherly love is loving your neighbor as yourself, fatherly love is loving people as Jesus loved us, seeing them with the eyes with which God sees them [140:5.1, 140:5.3]. All of this is a way of happiness rooted not in law but in faith and love [140:5.23].

q306.question: Why did Jesus not offer concrete solutions to the political, social, and economic problems of his day?
q306.answer:
The Urantia Book states plainly that Jesus was neither a political reformer nor an economic reformer, and that in his public teachings he ignored the civic, social, and economic realms. His concern was solely with the principles of man's inner and personal spiritual life [140:8.9-8.10]. This was not due to indifference but to his conviction that when people are renewed from within, each age can find better solutions for itself.

This teaching is recorded in a four-hour conversation that Jesus held with Peter, James, and John in a boat one Thursday afternoon after the ordination of the apostles [140:8.1].

1. Political Attitude: Not Turning Aside from His Mission

Jesus forbade the apostles to become embroiled in the tensions between the Jewish people and the Roman government, and, avoiding the political snares of his enemies, he answered: "⟦Q 140:8.9⟧Render to Caesar the things which are Caesar's and to God the things which are God's⟦/Q⟧." [140:8.9] He refused to have his attention diverted from his mission of establishing a new way of salvation, and in his personal life he duly observed all civil laws [140:8.9]. The Urantia Book explains that if he had come to reorganize the world, his teaching would have applied only to that age, and it warns against identifying Jesus' teachings with any political or economic theory or social system [140:8.10].

2. Social Attitude: The Individual, Not the Group

Jesus taught an active kindness that extends the range of one's neighbors to the whole world, but his concern was with the individual, not the group. He was not a sociologist, yet he worked to break down every form of selfish isolation and taught pure sympathy [140:8.11]. At the same time he pointed out that indiscriminate kindness may be the cause of social evils, and he instructed that the apostolic funds not be carelessly spent on alms [140:8.13]. He also taught nonresistance, but not the passive toleration of evildoing, and he recognized that civil government may use force to maintain order and justice. His teaching applied to the individual, not to the state [140:8.4-8.5].

3. Economic Attitude: Not Wealth but What Wealth Does

Jesus called attention to the injustice of the unequal distribution of wealth, but he offered no remedy. He made it clear that he was not opposed to wealth and property as such but to their unfair distribution [140:8.15]. The demand to give up their possessions was made only of the twelve apostles, and he never directed his followers to live in common [140:8.16]. "⟦Q 140:8.18⟧Não foi à riqueza que ele denunciou, mas ao que essa riqueza faz à maioria dos devotos dela.⟦/Q⟧." [140:8.18]

4. Why He Gave No Solutions

The Urantia Book explains that Jesus well knew that each age must develop its own solutions to its existing problems [140:8.17]. So if he were on earth today, he would disappoint many good people by taking no side, but he would remain in dignified aloofness and teach the way to perfect the inner spiritual life, so that people could solve their human problems far more competently [140:8.17]. Jesus would make all men Godlike and then stand by sympathetically while these sons of God solve their own problems [140:8.18]. Rather than offering solutions to nonreligious problems, he sought to stimulate insight into eternal realities and originality of living, and he was wholly concerned with the basic and permanent spiritual needs of the human race [140:8.31].

5. The Lesson for Our Lives

Jesus' teachings cannot be judged by the social or economic conditions of any one age; they contain the ideal principles of living near to God in all ages and on all worlds [140:8.2]. Yet no generation can escape the labor of finding how best to apply Jesus' life to its own problems [140:8.10]. The Master came to create in man a new spirit, a new will, endowed with a capacity for knowing the truth, experiencing compassion, and choosing goodness [140:8.32].

Summary

Rather than directly reforming political, social, and economic institutions, Jesus chose to plant a new spirit and a new will within the individual [140:8.9, 140:8.32]. Teachings bound to a particular system are confined to one age, but a personality determined to do God's will gains in every age the power to work out its own problems [140:8.10, 140:8.17]. He took issue not with wealth itself but with covetousness, not with social institutions but with selfish isolation [140:8.11, 140:8.18].

q307.question: How does the "spiritual unity" Jesus required of his apostles differ from the "uniformity" of everyone thinking the same thoughts?
q307.answer:
According to Paper 141 of The Urantia Book, Jesus did not want his apostles all to see alike or think alike. What he required of them was "spirit unity," experienced in their united dedication to the wholehearted doing of the will of the Father in heaven [141:5.1]. This unity differs fundamentally from uniformity in that it can be enjoyed together with the utmost diversity of thought, feeling, and action [141:5.2].

1. The Background of the Question

At one of the evening conferences at Amathus, James Zebedee asked how they might learn to see alike and thereby enjoy more harmony among themselves. Jesus was stirred within his spirit and replied: "⟦Q 141:5.1⟧James, James, when did I teach you that you should all see alike?⟦/Q⟧" [141:5.1] He said that he had come to proclaim spiritual liberty, to empower mortals to live individual lives of originality and freedom before God. And he declared that he did not desire social harmony and fraternal peace to be purchased by the sacrifice of free personality and spiritual originality [141:5.1].

2. The Source of Unity: The Identity of the Indwelling Spirit

Spiritual unity is derived from the consciousness that each one is indwelt by the spirit gift of the heavenly Father and is increasingly dominated by that spirit. The apostles' harmony was to grow out of the fact that the spirit hope of each of them is identical in origin, nature, and destiny [141:5.1]. That is, believers experience a perfected unity of spirit purpose and understanding through their mutual consciousness of the identity of the indwelling Paradise spirits within each of them [141:5.2]. The key point is that the ground of unity is not some outward rule or creed but the same spirit of the Father within.

3. Oneness amid Diversity

Jesus said that profound spiritual unity can be enjoyed even with the utmost diversity in intellectual thinking, temperamental feeling, and social conduct. Personalities may be refreshingly diverse and markedly different, yet their spiritual natures and the fruits of their worship and brotherly love can be so unified that those who observe them recognize the unity of their souls [141:5.2]. Each one may serve according to the manner of his own original endowment of mind, body, and soul, and yet achieve unity in the service of God [141:5.2]. Elsewhere too Jesus constantly urged his disciples not to press believers into set molds but to let each soul develop in its own way [140:8.26].

4. The Two Meanings of Unity

Jesus explained that spiritual unity implies two things [141:5.3].

A common motive of service: All desire above everything else to do the will of the Father in heaven.

A common goal of existence: All purpose to find the Father in heaven and to prove to the universe that they have become like him.

Where these two are the same, believers are spiritually one, even if they differ in theological interpretation or method.

5. A Warning against Creeds and Standardization

During the training of the apostles Jesus returned to this theme many times, saying that he did not want those who believed in him to become dogmatized and standardized, even according to the religious interpretations of good men. He also repeatedly warned against the formulation of creeds and the establishment of traditions as a means of guiding and controlling believers [141:5.4]. In the same spirit The Urantia Book says that the religion of Jesus did not crystallize in his day into creeds or theological laws [140:8.29].

Summary

Uniformity demands the same thoughts and the same forms, but spiritual unity arises from the consciousness that the same spirit of the Father dwells in each person, and from a common motive and goal: to do the Father's will and to become like him [141:5.1, 141:5.3]. So even with diversity of thought, temperament, and conduct, believers can be deeply one, and Jesus guarded against creeds and standardization in order to protect this liberty [141:5.2, 141:5.4].

q308.question: What actually happened in the story of the woman taken in adultery according to The Urantia Book, and why did Jesus not condemn her?
q308.answer:
Paper 162 of The Urantia Book relates this incident, which took place in front of the temple in Jerusalem at the feast of tabernacles, somewhat differently from the Gospels. It was less an effort to judge the woman's sin than a trap devised to bring Jesus into conflict with the Roman authorities or the Sanhedrin [162:3.3]. Jesus wrote in the sand and caused the accusers and conspirators to depart one by one, and then said to the woman left standing alone: "⟦Q 162:3.5⟧I know about you; neither do I condemn you. Go your way in peace⟦/Q⟧." [162:3.5] This woman, Hildana, forsook her wicked husband and joined herself to the disciples of the kingdom [162:3.5].

1. Correcting the Record

The Urantia Book says that the record of this episode as it has come down to us is distorted. That record suggests that Jesus dealt with the situation by implying that the Jewish religious leaders themselves were guilty of immorality, but Jesus knew that the scribes and Pharisees, though spiritually blind and bound by tradition, were among the most thoroughly moral men of that generation [162:3.1]. In fact it was hired agents of the Sanhedrin who dragged the woman before him, and they asked what he would do, since the law of Moses commands that such a woman be stoned [162:3.2].

2. A Threefold Trap

The enemies' plan was carefully laid [162:3.3].

If he said to stone her: Since the Jews could not carry out a death sentence without the approval of a Roman court, this would bring Jesus into conflict with the Roman rulers.

If he forbade it: They would accuse him before the Sanhedrin of setting himself up above Moses and the Jewish law.

If he kept silent: They would accuse him of cowardice.

But Jesus so managed the situation that the whole plot fell to pieces of its own sordid weight [162:3.3].

3. The Hidden Story: A Woman Used as Bait

The Urantia Book reveals this woman's circumstances. She was the wife of an inferior citizen of Nazareth, a man who had been a troublemaker in Jesus' youth, and after their marriage this husband forced his wife to earn their living by trafficking with her body. He had come up to Jerusalem for the feast and there had bargained with the hirelings of the Jewish rulers to betray his own wife, and they brought the woman and her partner in order to entrap Jesus [162:3.4]. Jesus recognized the husband standing behind the crowd and wrote a few words in the sand near him, and the husband departed in haste. Then he wrote again for the benefit of the accusers, and again for the woman's companion, and they all went away one by one [162:3.5].

4. The Meaning of "⟦Q 162:3.5⟧Neither Do I Condemn You⟦/Q⟧"

Jesus did not refrain from condemning the woman because he took sin lightly. When he ordained the apostles he taught them: "⟦Q 140:3.17⟧“Tendes a missão de salvar os homens, não de julgá-los.⟦/Q⟧." [140:3.17] And on social questions, the nearest he came to making sociological pronouncements was to say: "⟦Q 140:8.12⟧Judge not, that you be not judged⟦/Q⟧." [140:8.12] Moreover, in the divine eyes such a woman could appear as a soul more sinned against than sinning through her own desires. This is the same view the record takes of the Samaritan woman Nalda [143:5.8]. Jesus labored to teach the apostles that women of questionable morals could also choose God as their Father and become daughters of God [143:5.11].

5. The Balance of Forgiveness and Responsibility

A similar scene took place in the house of Simon the Pharisee. Jesus said to a woman of ill repute: "⟦Q 147:5.5⟧Woman, go in peace; your faith has saved you⟦/Q⟧." [147:5.5] And he explained that although this woman was in a lowly place now, her soul was moving progressively Godward [147:5.8]. Yet he solemnly warned that the Father in heaven is not a lax, loose, or foolishly indulgent parent who is ever ready to condone sin [147:5.9]. Not condemning is not permissiveness; it is a mercy that opens the opportunity to begin a new life. That Hildana actually left her husband and joined the disciples is the fruit of it [162:3.5].

Summary

The case of the adulterous woman was a trap set by agents of the Sanhedrin and the woman's own husband, and Jesus wisely brought the plot to nothing [162:3.3-3.4]. He did not condemn the woman because he came to save people rather than to judge them [140:3.17, 162:3.5], and his mercy was not a condoning of sin but the opening of a way for the soul to turn back to God [147:5.8-5.9].

q309.question: What did Jesus mean when he told Nicodemus about being "born from above," that is, being born of the spirit?
q309.answer:
According to Paper 142 of The Urantia Book, being born of the spirit is not some mysterious ritual or a momentary emotional experience; it is to choose wholeheartedly the guidance of the Father's spirit, which already dwells within a person, and to make the doing of the will of the Father in heaven one's only purpose in living [142:6.7]. When one does so, one enters the kingdom of God and begins to bear the fruits of the spirit in daily life.

1. Who Was Nicodemus?

Nicodemus was a wealthy and elderly member of the Jewish Sanhedrin. He was interested in Jesus' teachings, but fearing to be seen, he met Jesus privately by night at the home of Flavius [142:6.1]. He came not as an official representative of the Sanhedrin but out of personal and sincere interest, and Jesus received him calmly and with dignity, neither showing him special deference nor rebuffing or ridiculing him [142:6.2].

2. Jesus' Words: Born of the Flesh and Born of the Spirit

Jesus said: "⟦Q 142:6.4⟧“Em verdade, em verdade, eu te digo, Nicodemos, a menos que um homem tenha nascido do alto, ele não pode ver o Reino de Deus”.⟦/Q⟧." [142:6.4] Nicodemus asked in return how an old man could enter a second time into his mother's womb [142:6.4]. Jesus said that what is born of the flesh is flesh and what is born of the spirit is spirit, and he used the illustration of the wind. Just as we hear the rustle of the leaves but do not see the wind, and know not whence it comes or whither it goes, so the manifestations of one who is born of the spirit can be seen, but the spirit itself cannot be discerned with the eyes of the flesh [142:6.5].

3. The Way to Be Born of the Spirit

When Nicodemus asked how he could lay hold upon the spirit that was to remake him, Jesus answered: "⟦Q 142:6.7⟧“O espírito do Pai no céu já reside em ti.⟦/Q⟧." [142:6.7] Three steps are contained in these words [142:6.7].

Desiring to be led by the spirit: If one would be led by the spirit from above, very soon one would begin to see with the eyes of the spirit.

Choosing wholeheartedly: By the wholehearted choice of spirit guidance one is born of the spirit.

A change in the purpose of life: One's only purpose in living becomes doing the will of the Father in heaven, and one begins to bear in daily life the abundant fruits of the spirit.

In other words, the heart of the new birth is a decision of the will to co-operate with the spirit already dwelling within. Jesus also asked Nicodemus whether he had the courage to have faith in the Son of Man who came down from heaven [142:6.6].

4. What Nicodemus Lacked

The Urantia Book says that Nicodemus was proficient in self-development, self-control, and high moral qualities, and that he was refined and altruistic. But he did not know how to submit his will to the will of the divine Father as a little child is willing to submit to the guidance of a wise and loving earthly father [142:6.8]. It is by just such submission that a person truly becomes a son of God, a progressive heir of the eternal kingdom [142:6.8]. Moral excellence alone is not enough; entrusting oneself to the Father's will with childlike trust is the door of the new birth. This is also the meaning of Jesus' saying elsewhere that he wanted to set men free so that they might start out afresh, like little children, upon the new and better life [140:8.26].

5. Nicodemus Afterward

Nicodemus went away that day confused, but he developed faith sufficient to lay hold of the kingdom. He feebly protested when the Sanhedrin sought to condemn Jesus without a hearing, and later, when most of the disciples had fled in fear, he came forward with Joseph of Arimathea, confessed his faith, and claimed the body of Jesus [142:6.9].

Summary

To be born again from above is to choose wholeheartedly the guidance of the Father's spirit already dwelling within, making the doing of the Father's will one's only purpose in living [142:6.7]. Like the wind it is invisible, yet it is revealed in the fruits of life [142:6.5], and it begins not with moral achievement but with entrusting one's will to the Father's will in childlike trust [142:6.8].

q310.question: How does the "self-denial" taught by John the Baptist differ from the "self-control" (self-mastery) taught by Jesus?
q310.answer:
In Paper 143 of The Urantia Book, Andrew asked whether they should practice self-denial as John had taught them, or strive for the self-control of Jesus' teaching. Jesus answered that John's teaching, in accordance with the light and laws of his fathers, was "⟦Q 143:2.2⟧the religion of self-examination and self-denial⟦/Q⟧," but that he himself had come "⟦Q 143:2.2⟧with a new message of self-forgetfulness and self-control⟦/Q⟧" [143:2.2]. The difference between the two ways lies in the direction of the effort. One is the way of suppressing the self by external rules; the other is the way of being transformed within by the spirit, so that one comes naturally to rule the self.

1. The Self-Control Jesus Himself Displayed

The Urantia Book says that the Master was the perfected example of human self-control. When he was reviled, he reviled not; when he suffered, he uttered no threats against his tormentors; when he was denounced by his enemies, he simply committed himself to the righteous judgment of the Father in heaven [143:2.1]. Jesus said that "⟦Q 143:2.3⟧he who rules his own self is greater than he who captures a city⟦/Q⟧," and he taught that self-mastery is the measure of man's moral nature and the indicator of his spiritual development [143:2.3].

2. The Old Way and the New Way

The old way: One tries to suppress, to obey, and to conform to rules of living. One fasts and prays, and lives in fear of the bondage of the self and in the slavery of self-denial [143:2.3-2.4].

The new way: One is first transformed by the Spirit of Truth, and the inner soul is strengthened by the constant spiritual renewing of the mind, so that one receives the power to do the will of God certainly and joyfully [143:2.4]. The new creature of the rebirth of the spirit is taught to believe and rejoice [143:2.3].

Jesus said that personal faith in the promises of God makes a person a partaker of the divine nature, and since that spirit actually dwells within, one is no longer a slave of the flesh but a liberated son of the spirit. The new law of the spirit gives the liberty of self-mastery in place of the old law of self-denial [143:2.4].

3. An Honest Recognition of the Cause of Evil

Jesus pointed out that when people do evil they blame it on the influence of the evil one, but in reality they are often led astray by their own natural tendencies. People deceive themselves and easily fall into foolish fears, lusts, enslaving pleasures, envy, and even vengeance [143:2.5]. Self-control begins with honestly seeing this self-deception.

4. The Secret of Self-Mastery: Faith and the Indwelling Spirit

Salvation is accomplished not by self-righteous works of the flesh but by the regeneration of the spirit, and a person is justified by faith and received into fellowship by grace, not by fear and the self-denial of the flesh [143:2.6]. So cleansing oneself from the evils of mind and body is now no longer a duty but an exalted privilege [143:2.6]. Jesus said, "⟦Q 143:2.7⟧O vosso segredo da mestria e do controle sobre o ego está ligado à vossa fé no espírito residente, que sempre trabalha por amor.⟦/Q⟧," and added that even this saving faith is the gift of God [143:2.7]. He also said that it is the very goodness of God that leads men into true repentance [143:2.7].

5. Self-Control as the Fruit of the Spirit

Those who are born of the spirit are freed from the life of self-denial and from the self-conscious bondage of watching over the desires of the flesh, and they spontaneously show forth the fruits of the spirit in daily living. These fruits of the spirit are the very essence of the highest type of enjoyable self-control, the true self-mastery that is the height of mortal attainment on earth [143:2.8]. In the same vein The Urantia Book says that the religion of Jesus has no provisions for religious introspection, and that he taught not character building but character growth [140:8.27].

Summary

John's way was the way of self-denial, of examining and restraining the self; Jesus' way is the way of self-mastery, in which one forgets the self, is transformed by the spirit, and so comes to rule the self [143:2.2, 143:2.4]. Its power comes not from the strain of the will but from faith in the indwelling spirit, which works by love [143:2.7], and its result is not a suppressed life but the joyful liberty in which the fruits of the spirit spontaneously grow [143:2.8].

q311.question: What do Jesus' words about "living water" and "worship in spirit and in truth," spoken to the Samaritan woman Nalda at Jacob's well, mean?
q311.answer:
Paper 143 of The Urantia Book tells in detail of Jesus' meeting with Nalda, a woman of Sychar in Samaria, at Jacob's well. Here "living water" refers to the gift of the indwelling spirit, and "worship in spirit and in truth" means not a place or a ritual but the soul's direct personal relationship with the Father [143:5.10, 143:5.6]. This meeting was also the occasion on which Jesus made the first clear declaration on earth of his divinity and sonship [143:5.8].

1. Living Water: A Well Springing Up to Eternal Life

When Jesus asked for a drink, Nalda, surprised that a Jewish man should speak to a Samaritan woman, asked him why [143:5.2]. Jesus replied: "⟦Q 143:5.3⟧“Todos os que beberem dessa água terão sede novamente, mas quem beber da água do espírito vivo nunca mais terá sede.⟦/Q⟧." [143:5.3] He said that this living water would become in a person a well springing up even to eternal life [143:5.3]. When Nalda brought the people of the city, Jesus spoke further to them of the water of life, the gift of the indwelling spirit [143:5.10].

2. Repentance before the Truth That Awakened Her Soul

Nalda at first misunderstood Jesus' kindness, but when he commanded her to call her husband, she came to her senses [143:5.4]. The Urantia Book explains that she had been unjustly cast aside by her husband and, driven to extremity, had come to live with a Greek. She was ashamed and sincerely repentant [143:5.5]. Jesus did not say much to her, but his look and manner spread out the whole of her past life before her mind [143:5.13].

3. Sidestepping into Theological Debate

Nalda, while seeking personal help, sidestepped the question of her personal salvation by turning, as so many do, to a discussion of theology and philosophy. She asked whether Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem was the proper place of worship [143:5.5]. Jesus perceived that her soul was trying to avoid direct contact with its Maker, but he also saw the longing within her and answered patiently. He said that "⟦Q 143:5.6⟧the hour will soon come—even now is—when all sincere worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth⟦/Q⟧" [143:5.6], and that salvation comes not from knowing how or where others should worship but from receiving the living water into one's own heart [143:5.6].

4. "⟦Q 143:5.7⟧I Who Speak to You Am He⟦/Q⟧"

When Nalda turned again to general religious matters and spoke of the coming Deliverer, Jesus said with startling assurance, "⟦Q 143:5.7⟧I who speak to you am he⟦/Q⟧." [143:5.7] The Urantia Book emphasizes that this was the first direct declaration of his divinity and sonship, and that it was made to a Samaritan woman whom people regarded as of questionable morals. In the divine eyes she appeared as a human soul more sinned against than sinning, one who sincerely longed for salvation [143:5.8]. Jesus said to her, "⟦Q 143:5.9⟧Deus te perdoou.⟦/Q⟧," and told her that she would become a daughter of the Most High [143:5.9].

5. Continued Teaching on Spiritual Worship

At the evening meetings on Mount Gerizim, Jesus taught that true religion is the act of an individual soul in its self-conscious relations with the Creator [143:7.2]. Worship is the act of a son's personal communion with the divine Father, the act of the part identifying itself with the Whole, the finite with the Infinite [143:7.8]. The apostles found it hard to accept the teaching that even women of questionable morals had souls that could choose God as their Father [143:5.11].

Summary

Living water is the gift of the indwelling spirit, springing up to eternal life [143:5.3, 143:5.10], and worship in spirit and in truth is the soul's direct communion with the Father, beyond disputes over place and form [143:5.6, 143:7.8]. By first revealing himself to a woman whom society had shunned, Jesus showed that anyone can choose God as Father and become his child [143:5.8, 143:5.11].

q312.question: Does Jesus' saying "turn the other cheek" mean passively submitting to evil, or what does it teach?
q312.answer:
Paper 159 of The Urantia Book states plainly that this saying calls not for passive submission but for positive action for good. Jesus opposed even negative or purely passive nonresistance, and taught: "⟦Q 159:5.9⟧When an enemy smites you on one cheek, do not stand there dumb and passive but in positive attitude turn the other⟦/Q⟧" [159:5.9]. That is, one should do the best thing possible actively to lead the brother in error away from evil paths into a better life [159:5.9]. This is part of the "positive nature of Jesus' religion" that Jesus taught at Philadelphia during the Decapolis tour [159:5.1].

1. From a Negative Religion to a Positive Religion

The Urantia Book explains that Jesus breathed the spirit of positive action into the negative doctrines of the Jewish religion. Instead of passive conformity to ceremonial requirements, his religion consisted in actually doing what the gospel requires [159:5.8]. When reading the Scriptures too, Jesus chose the better portion and did not hesitate to reject the lesser. Even the exhortation "⟦Q 159:5.9⟧Love your neighbor as yourself⟦/Q⟧" he took by appropriating only the positive portion of a Scripture that forbade vengeance [159:5.9]. He changed the negative golden rule into a positive admonition, and he revealed a God who does not merely wait for the repentant sinner but goes out first to seek the lost sheep [159:5.16].

2. Three Ways of Meeting Evil

Jesus distinguished three ways of contending with and resisting evil [159:5.11-5.14].

Returning evil for evil: A positive but unrighteous method.

Suffering evil without complaint and without resistance: A purely negative method.

Returning good for evil: A positive and righteous method, in which one asserts the will, becomes master of the situation, and overcomes evil with good.

The way Jesus taught is the third. He abhorred both the idea of retaliation and the attitude of becoming a passive sufferer of injustice [159:5.11].

3. The Second Coat and the Second Mile

The saying about giving one's cloak also to him who takes the coat was not meant literally; it meant doing something positive to save the wrongdoer instead of following the retaliatory lesson of "⟦Q 159:5.11⟧an eye for an eye⟦/Q⟧" [159:5.11]. When asked what to do if a stranger forced one to carry his pack for a mile, Jesus said not to sit down and condemn him inwardly, but, if no more positive method was at hand, at least to carry the pack a second mile, for that would be a challenge to the unrighteous man [159:5.15]. Jesus did not advocate negative submission to those who would impose upon practitioners of nonresistance; he required that his followers be wise and alert and quick to overcome evil with good [159:5.10].

4. Connection with His Earlier Teaching

This teaching stands on the same line as what Jesus said from the beginning. He told the twelve apostles not to resist evil and not to combat injustice, yet he did not teach them passive toleration of evildoing [140:8.4]. He also said: "⟦Q 140:8.7⟧A wrong is not righted by vengeance. Do not make the mistake of fighting evil with its own weapons⟦/Q⟧." [140:8.7] His nonresistance concerned the personal attitude of the individual; he recognized that society may punish criminals and that civil government may use force to maintain justice [140:8.4-8.5]. At Tyre too he said again: "⟦Q 156:5.5⟧be not overcome by evil but rather overcome evil with good⟦/Q⟧." [156:5.5]

5. What It Means for the Believer's Life

Jesus never told his followers merely to bear their obligations patiently; he taught them to live up, with energy and enthusiasm, to the full measure of their responsibilities and privileges in the kingdom [159:5.10]. Turning the other cheek demands initiative and calls for a vigorous, active, and courageous expression of the believer's personality [159:5.9]. The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 159:5.10⟧Não esqueçais: o bem verdadeiro é, invariavelmente, mais poderoso do que o mal mais maligno.⟦/Q⟧." [159:5.10] Jesus himself so lived, and it is recorded that "⟦Q 159:5.10⟧he went about doing good⟦/Q⟧" [159:5.10].

Summary

The saying "turn the other cheek" does not mean to retreat helplessly before evil; it teaches a third way that is neither retaliation nor resignation, an active righteousness that overcomes evil with good [159:5.12-5.14]. Its purpose is not to protect oneself but to lead the erring brother into a better way [159:5.9], and it shows the essence of Jesus' religion, which calls not for negative prohibitions but for positive action [159:5.8].

q313.question: How did the sundown healing at Capernaum, in which 683 people were healed at once, come about, and why was Jesus reluctant to work miracles?
q313.answer:
Paper 145 of The Urantia Book describes in detail the "sundown healing" that took place at Capernaum early in A.D. 28. At the moment when Jesus, leaving the matter of healing to his Father's will, said that he desired to see his children made whole, the celestial host attending him came down, and 683 men, women, and children were healed of all their physical diseases [145:3.10]. But the one most surprised by this event was Jesus himself [145:3.11], and early the next morning he was deeply concerned about it, for a spiritual kingdom cannot be built upon miracles and physical healing [145:5.4].

1. The Background: A Stage Set by Rumor

That Sabbath afternoon a young man in the synagogue had an epileptic seizure, and when Jesus took him by the hand he revived. The Urantia Book explains that he was not possessed by an evil spirit but was an ordinary epileptic, and that he was not healed at that time, yet the people believed that Jesus had cast out a devil [145:2.12-2.13]. When the fever of Amatha, Peter's mother-in-law, happened to subside, the apostles too regarded it as a miracle and spread the report [145:2.15-2.16]. These incidents illustrate the typical way in which a miracle-minded generation made coincidences the occasion for miracles [145:2.17]. When the sun set, nearly a thousand people thronged before the house of Zebedee [145:3.6].

2. How the Healing Took Place

Seeing the suffering multitude, Jesus' human heart was deeply moved, and the divine compassion of the Creator Son was aroused. But he knew that he could not build an enduring spiritual movement on the foundation of purely material wonders, and it had been his consistent policy to refrain from exhibiting his creator prerogatives [145:3.7]. At that moment a retinue of seraphim, physical controllers, Life Carriers, and midwayers stood ready to act at a signal [145:3.8]. Jesus said that he desired to see his children made whole if it were his Father's will [145:3.9], and when his Personalized Adjuster instantly ruled that the act would not transgress the Father's will, the creative act took place. The Urantia Book explains: "⟦Q 145:3.11⟧Aquilo que um Filho Criador deseja, e que é a vontade do seu Pai, É.⟦/Q⟧." [145:3.11] No such mass healing ever took place again [145:3.11].

3. The Spiritual Results of the Miracle

Surprisingly, most of those who were healed received no lasting spiritual benefit from it, nor was the spiritual kingdom advanced in the hearts of the people [145:3.14]. The healing miracles were not part of the plan for proclaiming the kingdom; they were incidental, arising because a Creator was on earth possessed of divine mercy and human sympathy, and they rather caused Jesus much trouble by arousing prejudice and bringing unwanted notoriety [145:3.15]. After this event Jesus was as much a physician as a preacher [145:3.13].

4. The Dawn Prayer and the Decision

Jesus scarcely slept that night. Considering the danger that his mission of establishing the spiritual kingdom in the hearts of men would become subordinated to physical ministry, as his time was taken up with caring for the sick, he went out alone at dawn to seek wisdom and judgment [145:5.1]. When Andrew urged him to return, saying that everyone was seeking him, Jesus asked whether they were not thronging to him because their bodies had been healed rather than because of spiritual truth [145:5.6]. He said that teaching must not be crowded out by preoccupation with healing, and he left Capernaum to set out on the first public preaching tour [145:5.7-5.8]. Thomas said: "⟦Q 145:5.10⟧Seguimos um instrutor que não busca nenhuma glória para si próprio”.⟦/Q⟧." [145:5.10]

Summary

The healing of the 683 came about when the Personalized Adjuster and the celestial host responded to the compassion of Jesus, who desired that his suffering children be made whole insofar as the Father's will allowed [145:3.10-3.11]. Yet it brought no spiritual growth to most of the people, and Jesus made it clear that the kingdom must be built not on signs but on hearts that receive spiritual truth [145:3.14, 145:5.6]. This teaches us today to ground our faith not in astonishing experiences but in our relationship with the Father.

q314.question: What are evil, sin, and iniquity as Jesus explained them to Thomas, and is man by nature a sinner?
q314.answer:
In Paper 148 of The Urantia Book, Thomas asked why men must be born again of the spirit and what evil is [148:4.1]. Jesus explained three degrees of transgressing the Father's will by distinguishing evil, sin, and iniquity. The heart of the distinction is the difference in the "consciousness and intent" of the transgression. And Jesus said plainly: "⟦Q 148:4.8⟧“Os homens, de fato, são maus por natureza; mas não necessariamente pecadores.⟦/Q⟧." [148:4.8]

1. Three Definitions

Evil: The unconscious or unintended transgression of the divine law, the Father's will. Evil is also the measure of the imperfectness of obedience to the Father's will [148:4.3].

Sin: The conscious, knowing, and deliberate transgression of the Father's will. Sin is the measure of unwillingness to be divinely led [148:4.4].

Iniquity: The willful, determined, and persistent transgression of the Father's will. Iniquity is the measure of the continued rejection of the Father's loving plan of personality survival and of the Sons' ministry of salvation [148:4.5].

Jesus also told them not to confuse evil with "the evil one." The one commonly called the evil one is the son of self-love who knowingly went into rebellion against the Father's rule, and Jesus said that he had already overcome these rebels [148:4.2].

2. Imperfection Is Not Sin

Before being born again of the spirit, mortal man is subject to inherent evil tendencies, but such natural imperfections of behavior are neither sin nor iniquity. Man is only just beginning his long ascent to the perfection of the Paradise Father, and to be imperfect or partial in natural endowment is not sinful [148:4.6]. A person is never a child of the evil one unless he knowingly and deliberately chooses the paths of sin and the life of iniquity. Evil is inherent in the natural order of this world, but sin is an attitude of conscious rebellion brought into this world by those who fell from spiritual light into darkness [148:4.6].

3. A Correction of the Theory of the Fall

Jesus pointed out that Thomas was confused by the doctrines of the Greeks and the errors of the Persians. Because Thomas thought that mankind began with a perfect Adam and rapidly degenerated through sin, he did not understand the relationship between evil and sin [148:4.7]. Jesus said he had come to show that man is not going down from divine perfection to destruction, but that by entering the kingdom he is certainly ascending to God and divine perfection [148:4.9]. Any being who falls short of the eternal Father's ideals is potentially evil, but in no sense sinful, much less iniquitous [148:4.9].

4. Why the New Birth Is Needed, and Sonship

Why, then, must one be born again? Jesus said that the new birth, the baptism of the spirit, is essential to deliverance from evil and to entrance into the kingdom of heaven. But this does not detract from the fact that man is the son of God. The notion that man is estranged from the Father so that, as an alien or stepchild, he must seek legal adoption, comes from misunderstanding the Father and from ignorance of the origin, nature, and destiny of man [148:4.8]. Citing several passages of Scripture, Jesus said that just as the material part of the human father is in his own children, so a spiritual part of the heavenly Father is in every faith son of the kingdom [148:4.10]. Moreover, the presence of evil alone is a sufficient test for human ascension; sin is not essential to survival [148:5.2].

5. A Lesson for the Spiritual Life

This distinction protects us from two errors. One is to be gripped by fear, regarding our own imperfections as condemnation before God; the other is to take lightly the weight of choices made knowingly. Jesus honestly acknowledged that people are often led astray by their own natural tendencies [143:2.5], while he taught them to master the self by co-operating in faith with the indwelling spirit [143:2.7].

Summary

Evil is the imperfection of transgressing the Father's will unknowingly; sin is transgressing it knowingly and deliberately; and iniquity is transgressing it with persistent determination and rejecting the plan of salvation [148:4.3-4.5]. Because man is imperfect he is by nature exposed to evil, but he is not in himself a sinner; he is not a fallen being but one ascending to God [148:4.6, 148:4.9]. The new birth is the way by which we, already children of God, rise above evil and consciously choose the Father's will [148:4.8].

q315.question: Why does the God of love permit suffering, and how did Jesus interpret the story of Job?
q315.answer:
In Paper 148 of The Urantia Book, Nathaniel and John asked why the loving Father permits so many of his children to suffer, and why innocent people fall sick and are afflicted [148:5.1, 148:6.1]. The heart of Jesus' answer is that "⟦Q 148:5.3⟧the Father does not purposely afflict his children⟦/Q⟧" [148:5.3]. Suffering is not an arbitrary punishment sent by God; it arises from the imperfections of an evolving world and from the consequences of sin and rebellion.

1. The Three Sources of Suffering

Jesus summed up for John three reasons why man suffers [148:6.11].

Natural causes: The accidents that occur naturally in the course of time, and the imperfections of evil inherent in an immature physical existence.

The consequences of sin: The inevitable results of transgressing the laws of life and light.

The harvest of iniquity: Man reaps the results of his own persistence in rebellion against the righteous rule of heaven.

And Jesus added: "⟦Q 148:6.11⟧But man's miseries are not a personal visitation of divine judgment⟦/Q⟧." [148:6.11] He also explained that the natural order of this world has been upset more than once by the sinful adventures of those who rebelled against the Father's will, and that it will take ages to set this right [148:5.2].

2. Do Not Blame God, but Strive

Jesus affirmed that the Father does not send affliction as an arbitrary punishment for wrongdoing. The imperfections of evil are inherent, the penalties of sin are inevitable, and the consequences of iniquity are inexorable [148:5.3]. Therefore man should not blame God for the natural results of the life he chooses to live, and it is the Father's will that man should work persistently toward the betterment of his estate on earth [148:5.3]. Ignorant man tends to charge God with responsibility for everything he does not understand, but the Father is not personally responsible for all these things [148:5.4].

3. Job and His Three Friends

Jesus called the Book of Job a masterpiece of Semitic literature and interpreted it. The children of Abraham held that material prosperity was evidence of God's favor, but Jesus said that God loves the poor just as much as the rich [148:6.2]. A man reaps what he sows, yet human suffering is not always a punishment for past sin [148:6.3].

Eliphaz: He said that only the wicked suffer, and so Job must deserve punishment [148:6.4].

Bildad: He said that since Job's children had died, they must surely have been sinners [148:6.5].

Zophar: He said that God's ways are unsearchable, so there must be some hidden purpose [148:6.8].

Jesus judged that Job was altogether right when he challenged the doctrine that God afflicts children in order to punish their parents [148:6.10].

4. Job's Triumph and Jesus' Mission

Job did not obtain an intellectual answer, but in the midst of the collapse of his theological defenses he gained a vision of God, and there followed a peace of soul that passes all understanding [148:6.3]. After the great struggle between faith and doubt he cried out, "My Vindicator lives!" [148:6.9] Jesus said that Job longed for a humanlike God who understands the mortal estate, and that it was for just this reason that the Son of Man came in the flesh, to comfort all who must endure the sufferings of Job [148:6.7]. God speaks not from the whirlwind but within the human heart as a still, small voice, and Jesus said that "⟦Q 148:6.10⟧he has become what you are that he may make you what he is⟦/Q⟧" [148:6.10].

Summary

Suffering does not come as God's arbitrary punishment; it comes from the imperfections of an evolving world, the consequences of sin, and the harvest of rebellion [148:6.11]. Rather than blaming God, man should lessen suffering by intelligent effort [148:5.3], and like Job, even within the clouds of suffering, one can discover by faith the mercy and righteousness of the Father [148:6.11]. Jesus became as we are in order to reveal just such a Father [148:6.7].

q316.question: The Bible says "fear the Lord," so why did Jesus teach people to look upon God without fear?
q316.answer:
In Paper 149 of The Urantia Book, Philip put exactly this question to Jesus. The Scriptures teach us to "fear the Lord," he said, while the Master teaches us to look upon the Father in heaven without fear; how can the two be reconciled [149:6.1]? Jesus explained this not as a contradiction but as stages of growth. At first people could learn reverence only through fear, but he had come to reveal the Father's love, and he wished to lead people from reverence, through recognition and appreciation, to love [149:6.2-6.3].

1. The Changing Meaning of "the Fear of the Lord"

Jesus said: "⟦Q 149:6.3⟧“O ‘temor ao Senhor’ tem tido diferentes significados nas sucessivas eras; vindo do medo, passando pela angústia e o pavor, até a admiração e a reverência.⟦/Q⟧." [149:6.3] When man recognizes only the works of God, he is led to fear the Supreme; but when he begins to understand and experience the character and personality of the living God, he is led increasingly to love such a good and perfect Father. It was just this changing of the relation of man to God that constituted the mission of the Son of Man on earth [149:6.3].

2. An Explanation Drawn from a Child's Growth

Jesus explained that just as a little child must be admonished to honor his parents, but as he grows comes to love them for what they are rather than for what they have done, so man too must start from the fear of God and pass through reverence, dependence, and respect to a grateful and affectionate love [149:6.6]. Intelligent children do not fear their father in order to receive gifts from him; they love their father in response to the gifts they have already received [149:6.4]. And so he said: "⟦Q 149:6.4⟧A bondade de Deus conduz ao arrependimento; a beneficência de Deus conduz ao serviço; a misericórdia de Deus conduz à salvação; enquanto o amor de Deus conduz à adoração espontânea e inteligente e de todo o coração.⟦/Q⟧." [149:6.4]

3. From Fear of Power to Worship of Personality

The forefathers feared God because he was mighty and mysterious, but Jesus' disciples adore him because he is magnificent in love, plenteous in mercy, and glorious in truth. The power of God engenders fear, but the nobility and righteousness of his personality beget reverence, love, and willing worship [149:6.5]. Jesus said that he had come to proclaim love instead of fear, trust instead of dread, and the worship of love and gratitude instead of compulsory service. Yet he acknowledged that for those still in darkness the fear of the Lord is still the beginning of wisdom [149:6.5].

4. A New and Higher Commandment

In place of the old teaching to "⟦Q 149:6.7⟧fear God and keep his commandments⟦/Q⟧," Jesus gave a new commandment: to "⟦Q 149:6.7⟧love God and learn to do his will, for that is the highest privilege of the liberated sons of God⟦/Q⟧" [149:6.7]. In the kingdom of heaven that he proclaimed there is no high and mighty king; the kingdom is a divine family centered on the Father. So he told them to cease fearing God as a king or serving him as a master, and instead to revere him as the Creator, honor him as the Father of spirits, love him as a merciful protector, and ultimately worship him as a wise Father [149:6.8]. Earlier, in the same spirit, he had said that he wished to deliver the apostles from the bondage of slavishly serving a jealous and wrathful king-God [149:6.2].

5. True Humility and False Humility

Jesus pointed out that false humility and hypocrisy grow out of mistaken concepts of God. Man may by nature be a worm of the dust, but when the Father's spirit dwells within him, he becomes divine in destiny [149:6.9]. Humility before God is fitting in the depths of the heart, but the hypocrisy of humility put on to attract attention is childish and unworthy of the enlightened sons of the kingdom [149:6.10].

Summary

"⟦Q 149:6.3⟧The fear of the Lord⟦/Q⟧" is the first stage belonging to an age that did not yet know God well, and Jesus came to bring that reverence to completion in love, through recognition and appreciation [149:6.3]. The mature child worships the Father not because of his power but because of who he is [149:6.5-6.6]. Therefore the believer should learn the Father's will not with the fear of a slave but with the love of a liberated child [149:6.7].

q317.question: What is the significance of the "women's evangelistic corps," in which Jesus set apart ten women as teachers of the gospel?
q317.answer:
The Urantia Book counts among the most amazing and daring acts of Jesus' earth life the setting apart, in January of A.D. 28, of ten women for the ministry of the kingdom of heaven [150:1.1]. In an age when women were not even allowed on the main floor of the synagogue, he commissioned women as authorized teachers of the gospel and as ministers to the sick, and The Urantia Book calls this charge "⟦Q 150:1.3⟧the emancipation proclamation which set free all women and for all time⟦/Q⟧" [150:1.3].

1. Who Were Chosen

Jesus called to Bethsaida ten devout women who had served at the earlier encampment and at the tented infirmary. Neither they themselves nor those who had taught them had imagined that Jesus would ordain women as ministers [150:1.1]. Those chosen included Susanna, the daughter of the chazan of the Nazareth synagogue; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas; Martha, the elder sister of Andrew and Peter; Ruth, the eldest daughter of Matthew Levi; and Celta, the daughter of a Roman centurion; later Mary Magdalene and Rebecca, the daughter of Joseph of Arimathea, were added [150:1.1]. It is striking how different they were from one another in background, station, and nationality.

2. Self-Organized and Self-Supporting

Jesus permitted these women to form their own organization, and they chose Susanna as their leader and Joanna as their treasurer. At first Judas provided funds for their equipment, but from then on they supplied their own funds and never again received support [150:1.2]. They were an independent ministering body, on an equal footing with the apostles.

3. The Shock of the Times and the Response

Although the apostles had many times heard the Master say that "⟦Q 150:1.3⟧in the kingdom of heaven there is neither rich nor poor, free nor bond, male nor female, all are equally the sons and daughters of God⟦/Q⟧" [150:1.3], they were literally stunned when he actually commissioned women as religious teachers. The whole country was stirred up, and Jesus' enemies made great capital of it, but the women believers in the gospel stood stanchly behind their chosen sisters [150:1.3]. The Urantia Book says that to do this in an age when a man would not even greet his own wife in a public place, in defiance of the rabbinic teaching that it was better to burn the words of the law than to deliver them to women, was the most astonishing and revolutionary feature of Michael's earth mission [149:2.8]. In one generation Jesus lifted women out of the disrespectful oblivion of the ages [149:2.9]. The apostles too were shocked at first but soon grew accustomed to it, and Jesus taught clearly that women were to have equal rights with men in the kingdom [138:8.11].

4. The Growth and Contribution of the Women's Corps

This women's corps later grew greatly. The original twelve women trained a larger corps of fifty women in the art of home visitation and the care of the sick, and Perpetua, Peter's wife, took charge of the enlarged women's work [163:7.3]. During the Perean tour the women's corps, now numbering sixty-two, took over most of the ministry to the sick [165:0.2]. After the resurrection Mary Magdalene, as the chief teacher and public spokesman of the women's corps, played an important part in proclaiming the Master's resurrection [190:0.5]. After Pentecost, in the brotherhood of the kingdom, woman stood before God on an equality with man [194:3.14].

5. The Later History

This liberation was put into practice by the apostles immediately after Jesus' departure, and in the early church women teachers and ministers were recognized as deaconesses, but later generations fell back to the olden customs. Paul conceded it in theory but never really incorporated it into his own attitude [150:1.3]. The Urantia Book says it is a shame that the religion bearing Jesus' name lacked the moral courage to follow this noble example [149:2.9].

Summary

The commissioning of the women's evangelistic corps showed, not in words but in an institution, the gospel that men and women stand before God as equal sons and daughters [150:1.3]. Going against the prejudices of the age, Jesus gave women authority to teach and to serve, and they carried a great share of the ministry to the sick and of the proclamation of the resurrection [149:2.8, 165:0.2, 190:0.5]. This example remains a challenge to communities of faith today [149:2.9].

q318.question: Why did Jesus teach in parables, and how should parables be rightly interpreted?
q318.answer:
According to Paper 151 of The Urantia Book, after Jesus told the parable of the sower by the Sea of Galilee, he used parables more and more in his public teaching [151:2.8]. The reason was that parables convey truth to minds of different levels at the same time, opening the way for those who seek truth while giving opponents less occasion to find fault [151:3.1, 151:3.14]. Jesus also taught how to read parables rightly: a parable is not an allegory in which every detail has a hidden meaning, but a story that illustrates one central truth [151:2.5, 151:2.7].

1. Why He Spoke in Parables

When Matthew asked why he spoke in parables to those who were seeking the truth, Jesus answered that those who truly desire to enter the kingdom of heaven would discern the meaning and be saved, while those who sought to ensnare him would see and yet not see [151:1.3-1.4]. The next evening he explained that before people of varying intellectual levels and dispositions he could not speak different words to each group, but that by teaching through stories each one could interpret according to his own intellectual and spiritual endowments [151:3.1]. And when the Jerusalem leaders were trying to teach that his work was done with the help of devils, parables appealing to nature were the best refutation [151:3.14].

2. The Value of Parables

The advantages of parables that Jesus emphasized to the apostles are these:

Appealing to several levels at once: They stimulate the imagination, challenge discrimination, and provoke sympathy without antagonism [151:3.6].

From the known to the unknown: They introduce the spiritual and supermaterial by way of things material and natural [151:3.7].

Avoiding prejudice: They arouse a minimum of personal antagonism, gracefully implant new truth, and help toward impartial moral decisions [151:3.8].

Avoiding controversy: They make it possible to present startling truths while largely avoiding conflict with tradition or established authority [151:3.10].

Long remembered: When one later sees the same scene, the lesson comes back to mind [151:3.11].

Jesus advised against fables and allegories and recommended the free use of nature parables, and he frequently alluded to the natural as "⟦Q 151:3.3⟧the unreal and fleeting shadow of spirit realities⟦/Q⟧." [151:3.3]

3. The Interpretations of Peter and Nathaniel, and Thomas's Observation

Concerning the parable of the sower, Peter attached a meaning to every detail, taking the birds to be Satan, while Nathaniel offered a different interpretation, taking the birds to be habits of living and the desires of the flesh [151:2.2-2.3]. The apostles divided into two camps and engaged in heated debate [151:2.4]. Then Thomas reminded them of Jesus' earlier teaching: in an illustration one should choose a story suited to illustrate one central truth, and one should not try to make a spiritual application of every minor detail of the story [151:2.5]. Thomas said that the one great truth this parable teaches is that, however faithfully the gospel is preached, the results will appear in varying degrees according to conditions of environment beyond the minister's control [151:2.6]. Jesus praised him: "⟦Q 151:2.7⟧Well done, Thomas; you have discerned the true meaning of parables⟦/Q⟧" [151:2.7], and he said that Peter and Nathaniel had done them all equal good in showing the danger of turning his parables into allegories [151:2.7].

4. The Hearer's Responsibility

Jesus told them not only to consider how the multitude heard the truth but to take heed how they themselves heard. The spiritual law that to him who has more shall be given, and from him who has not shall be taken away even that which he thinks he has, applies also to the hearing of parables [151:3.1]. To reject the truth contained in a parable, one must consciously override one's own honest judgment [151:3.9].

Summary

Jesus taught in parables because they convey truth suited to each person's level, avoid prejudice and controversy, and open the way for those who seek truth [151:3.1, 151:3.6-3.10]. To read a parable rightly, one should grasp the one central truth the story points to instead of searching for hidden meanings in every detail [151:2.5-2.7]. And above all, we must look to how we ourselves are hearing [151:3.1].

q319.question: When the multitude wanted to make Jesus king after the feeding of the five thousand, why did he refuse, and what was the "Capernaum crisis" that followed?
q319.answer:
Papers 152 and 153 of The Urantia Book record the feeding of the five thousand and the "Capernaum crisis" that followed it as one of the greatest turning points in Jesus' public life. After the multitude had eaten their fill they wanted to make him king, but Jesus firmly refused, saying: "⟦Q 152:3.2⟧“Meus filhos, a vossa intenção é boa, mas tendes uma visão curta e uma mente material”.⟦/Q⟧." [152:3.2] For his kingdom was not of this world but a spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God [152:3.2]. With this refusal and the synagogue sermon that followed, popular favor ebbed away like a tide, and the work of the kingdom became more concentrated on winning genuine spiritual converts [153:1.2].

1. The Miracle of Feeding the Five Thousand

When the food of the multitude that had followed Jesus for three days ran out, Jesus said that he did not want to send them away like sheep without a shepherd, and he distributed bread and fishes so that all were filled [152:2.7-2.9]. The Urantia Book explains that this was the first and only nature miracle Jesus performed as a result of conscious preplanning, and that Michael multiplied the food elements as he always does, except that the time factor and the visible life channel were eliminated [152:2.10]. This too came about through the combination of human pity and creative power [152:3.1].

2. Why He Refused to Be King

The Jews had long been taught that when the Messiah came the bread of life would be given them, as manna in the wilderness, and in the eyes of the well-fed multitude the power to feed carried with it the right to rule. So they shouted, "Make him king!" [152:3.1] Jesus pointed out that they wanted to make him king not because their souls had been lighted with truth but because their stomachs had been filled with bread, and he said that if they must have a king, let the Father of lights be enthroned in the heart of each of them [152:3.2]. At these words many turned away, and of the five thousand only about five hundred followed him to the end [152:3.3, 152:5.2].

3. Miracles Do Not Win Souls

Jesus made the apostles understand that miracles and material wonders do not win souls for the spiritual kingdom. The multitude had received food, but they did not hunger for the bread of life or thirst for the water of righteousness; instead they wanted to make him king so as to go on getting bread without labor [152:5.4]. This miracle did not advance the gospel among the lukewarm believers; rather it brought to a climax the miracle-seeking and king-craving of his close disciples, and it prepared the way for the more spiritual proclamation of the final year [152:5.6].

4. The "Epochal Sermon" in the Capernaum Synagogue

On the following Sabbath, as Pharisees and Sadducees from Jerusalem looked on, Jesus openly attacked the material concept of the Messiah in the Capernaum synagogue [153:1.1-1.2]. He told them that they had followed him not for truth but to get more bread for which they had not labored, and said: "⟦Q 153:2.7⟧hanker not after the meat which perishes but rather seek for the spiritual food that nourishes even to eternal life⟦/Q⟧" [153:2.6-2.7]. And he declared that the manna of Moses was earthly bread, while he himself was the bread of life come down from heaven [153:2.8]. This bread of life was his own combined nature of God and man, the revelation that the Father is in the Son and the Son is one with the Father [153:2.12]. He urged the congregation to choose this day whom they would serve [153:2.5].

5. The Sifting and Those Who Remained

That night came the report that about one third of the evangelists had deserted the cause [153:5.2]. Jesus told the discouraged apostles that this sifting was inevitable, and that they should not fear the kingdom shaking off the lukewarm multitudes and halfhearted disciples [153:5.3]. He encouraged them: "⟦Q 153:5.4⟧it is the spirit that quickens; the flesh and all that pertains thereto is of little profit⟦/Q⟧." [153:5.4] Because Jesus knew that people are made ready for crisis decisions through the slow process of repeated choosing between good and evil, he gave his disciples this rehearsal in disappointment [153:1.3].

Summary

Jesus refused to be king of a multitude whose bellies had been filled with bread, because his kingdom is not a material throne but a spiritual brotherhood that enthrones the Father in each person's heart [152:3.2]. In the Capernaum crisis that followed, he declared himself the bread of life and called on people to choose; as a result many left, but those who remained were tempered in a deeper faith [153:2.5, 153:2.12, 153:5.3]. This event shows that faith must stand not on signs or advantage but on spiritual truth [152:5.4].

q320.question: If God does not lead people into temptation, where does temptation come from, and how did Jesus teach us to overcome it?
q320.answer:
According to Paper 156 of The Urantia Book, one evening during the stay at Tyre, Nathaniel asked why we pray not to be led into temptation if God never leads anyone into temptation [156:5.3]. Jesus answered that because the forefathers sought to see the hand of God in everything, they came to believe that God led them into temptation too, but that in fact "⟦Q 156:5.4⟧men are all too often led into temptation by the urge of their own selfishness and by the impulses of their animal natures⟦/Q⟧" [156:5.4]. And he taught that the way to overcome temptation is not suppression by the will but a spiritual transformation in which one comes truly to love what is higher [156:5.5].

1. The Old View and the New Understanding of the Source of Temptation

Jesus explained that the forefathers connected God with both good and evil, thinking that he softened the heart of Moses and hardened the heart of Pharaoh. When people felt a strong urge they were in the habit of saying, "⟦Q 156:5.4⟧The Lord spoke to me⟦/Q⟧," and so they believed that God led them into temptation for testing, punishing, or strengthening [156:5.4]. But disciples who have come to know the Father rightly know that most temptation comes from their own selfishness and animal nature [156:5.4]. This agrees with what Jesus said elsewhere, that people blame evil on the evil one when in fact they have been led astray by their own natural tendencies [143:2.5].

2. The First Method: Recognize Honestly and Redirect Energies

Jesus advised that when one is tempted, one should recognize the temptation honestly for just what it is, and intelligently redirect the energies of spirit, mind, and body that are seeking expression into higher channels and toward more idealistic goals. In this way one can transform temptations into the highest types of uplifting ministry while almost wholly avoiding wasteful conflicts between the animal and spiritual natures [156:5.4].

3. The Folly of Fighting with Willpower Alone

Jesus warned against the folly of trying to supplant one desire by another through the mere force of the will. To be truly triumphant, one must come to the place of spiritual advantage where one has truly developed an actual interest in, and love for, the higher conduct one wishes to substitute [156:5.5]. Then, instead of the heavy burden of suppressing desires, one is delivered through spiritual transformation, and the old and inferior are forgotten in the love for the new and superior. Jesus said, "⟦Q 156:5.5⟧Há um forte poder de eliminação na energia de uma afeição espiritual nova e sincera.⟦/Q⟧," and told them not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good [156:5.5]. This is the same principle by which he taught self-mastery as the fruit of the spirit in place of John's self-denial [143:2.8].

4. The White Lily and the Carpenter

That same day Jesus first told the story of the white lily. Just as the lily, though its roots are in the dark mire, lifts its blossom high into the sunlight, so man, though his origin is in the soil of animal nature, can by faith lift his spiritual nature into the sunlight of heavenly truth and bear the fruits of the spirit [156:5.1]. He also told them not to be like the foolish carpenter who wastes his time squaring rotten timbers, but to make the intellectual and moral foundations of character strong enough to support the superstructure of the spiritual nature [156:5.2].

5. The Attitude after a Fall

Jesus told them not to become discouraged by the discovery that they are human. Human nature may tend toward evil, but it is not inherently sinful, and "⟦Q 156:5.8⟧Os erros que não conseguirdes esquecer no tempo serão esquecidos na eternidade.⟦/Q⟧." [156:5.8] A soul should not be judged by a single unfortunate episode, for spiritual destiny is determined solely by spiritual longings and purposes [156:5.9]. The true believer finds that as he lives day by day, it becomes easier to do right [156:5.13].

Summary

Temptation comes not from God but mainly from our own selfishness and animal nature [156:5.4]. Jesus taught us to acknowledge it honestly and redirect our energies toward higher goals, overcoming it not by suppressing it with the will but by a spiritual transformation in which we come truly to love what is higher [156:5.4-5.5]. Even when we fall we should not lose heart, but keep walking the way of overcoming evil with good, with our eyes on our eternal destiny [156:5.8-5.9].

q321.question: What is the significance of Peter's confession and the transfiguration on Mount Hermon in the life of Jesus, and who appeared at the transfiguration?
q321.answer:
The Urantia Book regards Peter's confession on the way to Caesarea-Philippi and the transfiguration on Mount Hermon six days later as the two events that opened the final phase of Jesus' public life. In Peter's confession the apostles for the first time clearly acknowledged Jesus not merely as the deliverer of the nation but as the Son of the living God [157:5.1], and at the transfiguration Jesus received from universe representatives the acknowledgment that his bestowal mission had been fulfilled, yet he decided, following the Father's will, to carry the mortal bestowal through to the end [158:3.5]. And the two beings who appeared at that time were not Moses and Elijah, as Peter supposed, but in fact Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek [158:1.8].

1. "⟦Q 157:3.5⟧Who Say You That I Am?⟦/Q⟧"

As they paused for lunch on the way, Jesus for the first time asked a question concerning himself: "⟦Q 157:3.3⟧Who do men say that I am?⟦/Q⟧" [157:3.3] The apostles reported that people regarded him as a prophet or as John the Baptist, or compared him with Moses or Elijah, and when Jesus asked, "⟦Q 157:3.5⟧But who say you that I am?⟦/Q⟧" Peter sprang to his feet and exclaimed: "⟦Q 157:3.5⟧You are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God⟦/Q⟧." And the eleven apostles arose to their feet with one accord to show their agreement [157:3.5]. Jesus said that this had been revealed by the Father, yet he charged them for the time being to tell no one [157:3.6].

2. What Was New in the Confession: The Recognition of Divinity

The apostles had often regarded Jesus as the Messiah before, but the Jewish concept of the deliverer did not include the idea that he would be divine. The Messiah was thought of as "the anointed one," not as "⟦Q 157:5.1⟧the Son of God⟦/Q⟧" [157:5.1]. Up to that time Jesus had tried to modify the concept of the Messiah, but finding this difficult, he chose the way of boldly acknowledging his divinity [157:5.2]. For three years he had called himself "⟦Q 157:5.1⟧the Son of Man⟦/Q⟧"; now he revealed that he was the Son of God and decided to build the kingdom of heaven upon the combined natures of the Son of Man and the Son of God [157:5.3].

3. What Happened on Mount Hermon

Six days later Jesus went up Mount Hermon with Peter, James, and John [158:1.1]. There he held a conference with Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek, and in the night the apostles saw Jesus shining with a heavenly light and conversing with two brilliant beings. The physical controllers, at Jesus' request, had arranged for the apostles to witness the scene [158:1.6, 158:1.8]. In his confusion Peter proposed building three tabernacles [158:1.9], and as a silvery cloud overshadowed them, a voice was heard saying: "⟦Q 158:1.10⟧“Este é o Meu Filho amado; dai ouvidos a ele”.⟦/Q⟧." [158:1.10]

4. The Meaning of the Transfiguration

The Urantia Book explains that the transfiguration was the occasion for the following:

The acknowledgment of the Eternal Son: The Eternal Mother-Son accepted the fullness of Michael's incarnation bestowal, and Gabriel brought that assurance [158:3.2].

The testimony of the Infinite Spirit: The universe representative of the Infinite Spirit, through the Father Melchizedek, testified to satisfaction with the fullness of the bestowal [158:3.3].

The testimony of the Father: The Father did not indicate that the bestowal was finished; only his unseen presence, through the Personalized Adjuster, testified that this was his beloved Son [158:3.4].

On this day Jesus could have given up the struggle and returned to the rule of his universe, but he chose to fill up the last measure of the Father's present will. The three apostles witnessed his refusal to accept full universe authority [158:1.4].

5. The Faith of the Apostles

The apostles' faith rose to its height at the feeding of the five thousand and then fell almost to zero; after Jesus acknowledged his divinity it again reached its highest point and then slowly declined, rising only after the resurrection, the third rally [158:1.5]. For the three apostles the transfiguration was the event announcing that the Master, as Son of God and Son of Man, had entered the final phase of his earth career [158:3.5].

Summary

Peter's confession was the first clear acknowledgment of Jesus' divinity, and on this occasion Jesus decided to build the kingdom upon the combined natures of the Son of Man and the Son of God [157:5.1, 157:5.3]. At the transfiguration Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek bore witness to the fullness of the bestowal, but instead of receiving universe authority Jesus chose, according to the Father's will, to walk the mortal path to the end [158:1.4, 158:3.5].

q322.question: Who was Rodan, the Greek philosopher of Alexandria, and what is his philosophy of the "art of living" and "maturity"?
q322.answer:
Rodan was a Greek philosopher from Alexandria who, during a week in September of A.D. 29 when the apostles were away on vacation, gave ten lectures at Magadan to Nathaniel, Thomas, and a group of about two dozen believers [160:0.1, 160:1.1]. The Urantia Book introduces him as "⟦Q 160:5.14⟧the Greek philosopher, one of the greatest of his race, who had become a believer in the gospel of Jesus⟦/Q⟧" [160:5.14]. His lectures are not the direct teaching of Jesus but a philosophy of living set forth by a philosopher in the light of the gospel, yet they contain deep insight into the maturing of personality, and so they were included in this revelation.

1. Urges, Desires, and Allurements: The Three Driving Forces of Life

Rodan held that human life is made up of three driving forces: urges, desires, and allurements. Strong character is formed when one sublimates natural urges into the social arts of living, transmutes present desires into higher longings, and transfers the allurement of familiar ideas to the realm of yet undiscovered ideals [160:1.2]. The more complex civilization becomes, the more difficult the art of living becomes, and mankind must learn the art of living anew every ten generations [160:1.3]. He said: "⟦Q 160:1.6⟧O desencorajamento, a preocupação e a indolência são evidências claras de imaturidade moral.⟦/Q⟧." [160:1.6]

2. Problem Solving and the Withdrawal of Worship

Rodan defined successful living as the art of mastering dependable techniques for solving common problems, and he said that the first step is to locate the difficulty and frankly acknowledge its nature [160:1.7]. And he confessed that the greatest method of problem solving he had learned from Jesus was "⟦Q 160:1.10⟧the isolation of worshipful meditation⟦/Q⟧" [160:1.10]. This worship gives a relaxation that renews the mind, an illumination that inspires the soul, courage to face one's problems, and a self-understanding that obliterates fear [160:1.12]. He also said that prejudice is inseparable from selfishness and can be eliminated through service to a cause greater than the self, the search for God [160:1.13].

3. Friendship and Marriage: The Art of Living Together

Rodan held that human beings are able to develop personality because they can communicate meanings, values, and ideals through symbols [160:2.1-2.2]. He said that friendship and relationships of mutual affection promote the higher factors of the art of living, and he named four of them.

Mutual self-expression and self-understanding: Noble impulses often die for lack of someone to hear them, and the most ideal of such relationships is the friendship of man and woman in an intelligent marriage [160:2.6].
