Union of souls: Pooling one another's insights helps to avoid the bias of a single viewpoint. This is why Jesus always sent out his messengers two by two [160:2.7].

Enthusiasm for living: Isolation exhausts the energy of the soul, but friendship adds joy [160:2.8].

Defense against evil: Association cannot turn evil into righteousness, but it greatly lessens its sting [160:2.9].

4. Tact and Tolerance, and the Art of Defeat

Rodan said that when we battle for the right, both the victor and the vanquished often sustain defeat, and he passed on what he had heard the Master say, that the "⟦Q 160:3.4⟧wise man, when seeking entrance through the locked door, would not destroy the door but rather would seek for the key wherewith to unlock it⟦/Q⟧." [160:3.4] He also said that a noble soul learns the art of defeat and knows how to lose cheerfully [160:4.13], and that wisdom is gained only through the experience of adjusting to the consequences of failure [160:4.14]. To one who seeks God, failure is only an educational episode in the eternal adventure [160:4.15].

5. The Religion of Ideals

Rodan held that the social character of true religion lies in its seeking to convert the individual and to transform the world [160:5.5]. He saw that the religion of Jesus calls for living spiritual experience [160:5.12], and moved by Jesus' assurance that the ideals of spirit reality are attainable, he professed: "⟦Q 160:5.8⟧My brethren, I am a believer⟦/Q⟧" [160:5.8]. He said that his philosophy had given him the urge toward maturity but lacked certainty of direction, and that the gospel of Jesus supplied this by fixing the goal [160:1.15].

Summary

Rodan's philosophy speaks of the "art of living" that sublimates urges and desires into higher ideals, of the growth of personality through friendship and marriage, of the wisdom of tact, tolerance, and the endurance of defeat, and of a maturity that draws strength from the withdrawal of worship [160:1.2, 160:1.10, 160:2.5, 160:4.13]. He held that the goal of all this maturing becomes stable only when one accepts the living God as the eternal goal [160:1.14].

q323.question: Through the story of the rich young man Matadormus and the parable of the rich fool, what did Jesus teach about wealth?
q323.answer:
Papers 163 and 165 of The Urantia Book present Jesus' teaching on wealth in several scenes. Its core is this: "⟦Q 163:2.10⟧As riquezas não têm nenhuma relação direta com a entrada no Reino do céu, mas o amor pela riqueza tem.⟦/Q⟧." [163:2.10] Jesus never taught that the possession of wealth is in itself a sin [163:2.11]; what he took issue with was wealth's becoming a person's master and obscuring the spiritual vision of the soul [165:4.6].

1. The Rich Young Man Matadormus

About the time of the ordination of the seventy, Matadormus, a wealthy young man and a member of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, asked to become one of the seventy messengers [163:2.4]. Jesus looked upon him with great love and told him that to become a messenger he must sell all that he had, distribute it, and follow him [163:2.5]. He went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. He had been brought up to believe that wealth was the token of God's favor [163:2.6]. The Urantia Book explains that what Jesus wanted was to deliver him not from his wealth as such but from the love of wealth, and that the requirement to give up all possessions applied only to the apostles and the seventy [163:2.6]. It also says that nearly every person holds on to some one thing that is cherished, and that entrance into the kingdom requires it as part of the price of admission [163:2.7]. The forces of the spiritual world do not coerce a person but allow him to go the way of his own choosing [163:2.8].

2. The True Meaning of "a Camel through the Eye of a Needle"

Jesus told the apostles how hard it is for those who have riches fully to enter the kingdom, and when Peter in astonishment asked who then could be saved, he answered: "⟦Q 163:3.2⟧all who put their trust in riches shall hardly enter into the spiritual life that leads to eternal progress⟦/Q⟧." [163:3.2] Yet with God all things are possible [163:3.2]. Jesus also said that the Father requires that the affections of his children be pure and undivided, and that if wealth does not invade the precincts of the soul, it is of little consequence in the spiritual life [163:3.3].

3. A Dispute over Inheritance and the Parable of the Rich Fool

In Perea, when a young man asked Jesus to help with the division of an inheritance with his brother, Jesus said that he was not a divider in such material matters and warned against covetousness. He said, "⟦Q 165:4.1⟧a man's life consists not in the abundance of the things which he may possess⟦/Q⟧," and that wealth in itself is not a curse, but the love of riches blinds the soul to spiritual realities [165:4.1]. Then he told the parable of the rich fool who meant to build greater barns, store up his wealth, and take his ease, but whose soul was required of him that very night; this man "⟦Q 165:4.3⟧had failed to lay up treasures in heaven for the satisfaction of the spirit and for the salvation of the soul⟦/Q⟧" [165:4.2-4.3].

4. Honest Wealth and the Spirit of Stewardship

To the question whether it is a sin to possess honest wealth, Jesus answered that it is not a sin to have honorable wealth, but it is a sin if it becomes a treasure that absorbs one's interests and diverts one's affections from the spiritual pursuits of the kingdom [165:4.5]. He said that there is a great difference between wealth that leads to covetousness and wealth that is held and dispensed in the spirit of stewardship, and he charged them: "⟦Q 165:4.6⟧Nunca deixeis de reconhecer o perigo de que a riqueza se converta na vossa dona, em vez de converter-se na vossa serva”.⟦/Q⟧." [165:4.5-4.6] One who has gained great wealth must answer at the judgment at least three questions: how much he accumulated, how he obtained it, and how he used it [165:4.10-4.13]. Jesus regarded the wise investment of surplus earnings as legitimate provision, but he repeatedly condemned the unfair exploitation of the weak by the strong and shrewd [163:2.11]. Nor did he condone idleness or indifference to the support of one's family [165:4.7].

Summary

Jesus did not require everyone to give up their wealth; he required it only of the apostles and the seventy [163:2.11]. The focus of his teaching is that the love of wealth and trust placed in riches separate the soul from God [163:2.10, 163:3.2]. Wealth should be a servant governed in the spirit of stewardship, and material things must always be subordinate to the welfare of the soul and to spiritual progress [165:4.6-4.7].

q324.question: Are accidents, disasters, and diseases God's punishment or providence? Don't angels prevent accidents?
q324.answer:
In Paper 166 of The Urantia Book, Thomas asked whether spirit beings take part in particular events of the material world, and whether angels or other spirit beings could prevent accidents [166:4.1]. Jesus' answer was clear. The idea that prosperity is a sign of God's approval and adversity proof of his displeasure is a superstition [166:4.3], and those who meet with accidents are not greater sinners but are "⟦Q 166:4.4⟧simply innocent victims of one of the accidents of time⟦/Q⟧" [166:4.4]. Likewise, disease is the result of material causes [166:4.10].

1. What Jesus' Own Life Showed

Jesus first reminded Thomas that the Son of Man, while living with them, had consistently refused to use heavenly powers for his own sustenance. They had all lived by the same means as all other people, and apart from the revelation of the Father and the occasional healing of afflicted children, they had seen no display of spiritual power in the material world [166:4.2]. That is, spirit beings do not continually manipulate the physical events of daily life to prevent accidents.

2. The Tower of Siloam and the Galileans

Jesus cited two events well known to the people of his day: Pilate's mingling of the blood of certain Galileans with the sacrifices, and the fall of the tower of Siloam, which killed eighteen men. He declared that these victims were not greater sinners than others [166:4.4]. The Father causes his rain to fall on the just and the unjust, and his sun to shine on the righteous and the unrighteous alike [166:4.4]. Jesus also told them to observe how much more gladly the poor receive the gospel, and asked why, if wealth were a proof of favor, the rich reject this good news so [166:4.3].

3. Three Kinds of Events in Life

Jesus divided the events that may occur in life into three kinds [166:4.5-4.8].

Ordinary events: Things that are part of the life one lives on earth together with one's fellows.

Accidents and misfortunes of nature: Becoming a victim of an accident of nature or of the mishaps of men, which are not foreordained or brought about by spiritual forces.

Results of following law: Reaping the harvest of one's efforts to comply with the natural laws that govern this world.

To illustrate the third, he told of a gardener who, instead of cutting down a barren fig tree, left it one more year, dug about it and fertilized it, and at last saw an abundant harvest. They had complied with the laws of fruitfulness [166:4.9].

4. On Sickness and Disability

Jesus said: "⟦Q 166:4.10⟧health is not the smile of heaven, neither is affliction the frown of God⟦/Q⟧." [166:4.10] When Nathaniel asked about a man born blind, whose sin had caused it, Jesus answered that neither the man nor his parents had sinned, and that the blindness had come about in the natural course of events [164:3.2, 164:3.7]. The rabbis of the day taught that all congenital blindness was due to sin [164:3.3], and Jesus repeatedly warned the apostles to avoid the common tendency to attribute spiritual causes to ordinary physical events [164:3.6]. The Urantia Book says that Jesus had the courage to teach that natural catastrophes and the accidents of time are not divine judgments or mysterious dealings of Providence [149:2.10].

5. The Difference between Material Blessings and Spiritual Gifts

Jesus explained that the Father bestows material things upon people without discrimination, but that spiritual gifts are limited by the capacity of the receiver, that is, by faith and the willingness to follow the Father's will [166:4.11]. Just as accidents and illness are not signs of God's will, neither are health and prosperity signs of one's spiritual state. Where God's favor is truly revealed is within the soul that has been opened by faith.

Summary

Accidents, disasters, and diseases are not God's punishment or hidden providence; they are accidents of time occurring in an evolving material world, or the results of material causes [166:4.4, 166:4.7, 166:4.10]. Jesus showed by his own life that spirit beings do not continually intervene in the physical events of daily life [166:4.2], and people can change outcomes by wisely following natural law [166:4.9]. The Father's true gift is the spiritual endowment given to the soul through faith [166:4.11].
